level1.text: An example household uses $3000\,\text{kWh}$ of electricity a year. The electricity is produced with hydropower, whose life-cycle emission factor is $24\,\text{g/kWh}$. How much carbon dioxide equivalent is produced per year by the household's electricity use? Give the answer in kilograms.

An electric sauna heater uses $3.0\,\text{kWh}$ of electricity in one sauna session. The electricity is produced with coal, whose life-cycle emission factor is $820\,\text{g/kWh}$. How much carbon dioxide equivalent is produced by one sauna session? Give the answer in kilograms.

An electric car uses $18\,\text{kWh}$ of electricity over a distance of $100\,\text{km}$. The electricity used to charge the car has been produced with wind power, whose life-cycle emission factor is $12\,\text{g/kWh}$. How much carbon dioxide equivalent is produced per $100\,\text{km}$? Give the answer in grams.

The life-cycle emission factor of rooftop panels is $41\,\text{g/kWh}$ and that of natural gas electricity is $490\,\text{g/kWh}$. Both produce the same amount of electricity. How many times as large is the emission of natural gas electricity compared with that of rooftop panels?

A washing machine and a tumble dryer together use $2.4\,\text{kWh}$ of electricity for one load of laundry, and the electricity is produced with natural gas. Read the life-cycle emission factor of natural gas electricity from the bar chart in the figure. How much carbon dioxide equivalent is produced by one load of laundry? Give the answer in kilograms.
Which of the following best describes the natural greenhouse effect?
level1.answer: Greenhouse gases let the Sun's radiation through but slow down the escape of the ground's thermal radiation.

choices.text: The gases of the atmosphere reflect most of the Sun's radiation back into space before it reaches the ground.
choices.feedback: That is not so. Most of the Sun's radiation passes through the atmosphere to the ground and warms it. Greenhouse gases mainly affect the thermal radiation emitted by the ground.

choices.text: The atmosphere absorbs all of the Sun's radiation into itself and uses it to warm the ground from above.
choices.feedback: The atmosphere does not absorb all the radiation: most of the Sun's radiation reaches the ground directly and warms it.

choices.text: The atmosphere produces thermal energy itself and uses it to warm the ground both by day and by night.
choices.feedback: The atmosphere is not a source of energy. The energy that warms the ground comes from the Sun, and the atmosphere only slows down the escape of energy.

choices.text: Greenhouse gases let the Sun's radiation through but slow down the escape of the ground's thermal radiation.
choices.feedback: Correct: the ground is warmed by the Sun's radiation and emits thermal radiation, whose escape greenhouse gases slow down. That is why the mean surface temperature is about $+15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, while a simple radiative balance model gives an effective radiating temperature of about $-18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

level1.text: Which of the following statements concerns climate and not weather? The statements are examples, not measurement results.
level1.answer: In Oulu the mean temperature in January over the period 1991–2020 is about $-10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

choices.text: In Oulu the mean temperature in January over the period 1991–2020 is about $-10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
choices.feedback: Correct: climate is the long-term average and variation of weather in a given area, typically over at least thirty years.

choices.text: In Oulu on Tuesday morning there was a frost of $-10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and in the afternoon it sleeted.
choices.feedback: This describes the situation of one day in a given place, so it is weather. Weather changes from hour to hour and from day to day.

choices.text: This week's mean temperature in Finland was $3\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ higher than last week's.
choices.feedback: Comparing weeks describes a short period, so it is weather. We speak of climate only when we look at a long period.

choices.text: Last night $10\,\text{cm}$ of snow fell in Kuopio, and in the morning it was $-5\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
choices.feedback: This is a single event in a given place and time, so it is weather.

level1.text: An example school uses $40\,000\,\text{kWh}$ of electricity a year. The electricity is produced with nuclear power, whose life-cycle emission factor is $12\,\text{g/kWh}$. How much carbon dioxide equivalent is produced per year by the school's electricity use? Give the answer in kilograms.

level2.text: A power plant that uses biomass produces $2.0\,\text{GWh}$ of electricity in a month. The life-cycle emission factor of biomass electricity is $230\,\text{g/kWh}$. How many tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent are produced by a month of electricity production? Give the answer in tonnes.

An example household uses $3600\,\text{kWh}$ of electricity a year. The electricity was first produced with coal ($820\,\text{g/kWh}$), but the household switches to buying wind electricity ($12\,\text{g/kWh}$). By how many tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent do the yearly emissions decrease? Give the answer in tonnes.

The electricity production of a small factory produced $12\,\text{t}$ of carbon dioxide equivalent during a year. The electricity was produced with natural gas, whose emission factor is $490\,\text{g/kWh}$. How much electricity did the factory produce? Give the answer in kilowatt-hours.

The emission factor for the burning of petrol is $69\,\text{g/MJ}$. Give the emission factor in the unit $\text{g/kWh}$, when $1\,\text{kWh} = 3.6\,\text{MJ}$. Only burning is counted, not the whole life cycle.

The table shows the carbon dioxide concentration $c$ of the atmosphere in different years (yearly averages of the NOAA Mauna Loa measuring station, rounded to whole ppm values). Assume that the concentration grows steadily between the years $2005$ and $2020$, that is, the model is a straight line. By how many ppm does the concentration grow per year on average according to this model? Give the answer in the unit ppm/a.

level2.text:
The table shows the greenhouse gas emissions of an example country by sector in the years $2010$ and $2020$ in millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (example data, not statistics).

a) Calculate the total emissions in each year.

b) By how many per cent did the total emissions decrease from $2010$ to $2020$? Give the answer in per cent.

A student calculated the emission of electricity produced with coal: $m = 820\,\text{g/kWh} \cdot 2.0\,\text{kWh} = 1640$, and answered that the emission is $1640\,\text{kg}$. What is the error in the calculation?
level2.answer: The result $1640$ is in grams and not in kilograms, so the correct answer is $1.6\,\text{kg}$.

choices.text: The emission factor should be divided by the energy and not multiplied by it, which would give a smaller result.
choices.feedback: The emission is obtained by multiplying the emission factor by the energy, $m = e \cdot E$. The multiplication was correct: the unit $\text{g/kWh} \cdot \text{kWh}$ gives grams.

choices.text: The energy should be converted into megajoules before multiplying, because the factor contains a unit of energy.
choices.feedback: No conversion is needed, because the unit of the emission factor is $\text{g/kWh}$ and the energy is already in kilowatt-hours. The kilowatt-hours cancel directly.

choices.text: The result $1640$ is in grams and not in kilograms, so the correct answer is $1.6\,\text{kg}$.
choices.feedback: Correct: the kilowatt-hours cancel and grams are left. The student forgot the unit conversion, and the answer was a thousand times too large.

choices.text: The result $1640$ is in milligrams and not in grams, so the correct answer is $0.0016\,\text{kg}$.
choices.feedback: The unit $\text{g/kWh} \cdot \text{kWh}$ gives grams, not milligrams. The result $1640\,\text{g}$ is $1.6\,\text{kg}$.

level2.text: The table shows the yearly electricity production $E$ of an example power plant and its yearly life-cycle emission $m$ in carbon dioxide equivalents (example data, not statistics). The uncertainty of the emission value of each year is $\Delta m = 10\,\text{kt}$. Which of the following conclusions does the data in the table support?
level2.answer: The emission decreased from the year $2020$ to the year $2024$, because the difference $100\,\text{kt}$ is much larger than the uncertainty $10\,\text{kt}$.

data.caption: Production and emission of an example power plant (example data)

choices.text: The emission decreased already from the year $2020$ to the year $2021$, because the difference $5\,\text{kt}$ is larger than the uncertainty $10\,\text{kt}$.
choices.feedback: Wrong comparison with the uncertainty. The difference $520\,\text{kt} - 515\,\text{kt} = 5\,\text{kt}$ is smaller, not larger, than the uncertainty $10\,\text{kt}$, so it can come from mere variation in measurement and calculation. A decrease cannot be shown from this pair.

choices.text: The table proves that the emission decreased because the plant switched from coal to biomass; the difference is larger than the uncertainty.
choices.feedback: Over-interpreting the cause. The table has only the production and the emission, and no information about the fuel. The data show that the emission decreased, but not why: more efficient equipment or some other change would be just as good a cause.

choices.text: The emission decreased from the year $2020$ to the year $2024$, because the difference $100\,\text{kt}$ is much larger than the uncertainty $10\,\text{kt}$.
choices.feedback: Correct: the difference of the emissions of the years $2020$ and $2024$ is $520\,\text{kt} - 420\,\text{kt} = 100\,\text{kt}$, ten times the uncertainty $10\,\text{kt}$. The uncertainty ranges of the values, $510$–$530\,\text{kt}$ and $410$–$430\,\text{kt}$, do not overlap. So the decrease is probably real, even though the small differences between single years would stay within the uncertainty.

choices.text: The emission in the year $2034$ is only $170\,\text{kt}$, because the decrease continues at the same rate as in the years $2020$–$2024$.
choices.feedback: Extrapolating too far. The data cover only five years, and the prediction would reach ten years beyond them. The development of the emissions can change, for example if the way the plant produces or is used changes, so this trend does not justify such a long prediction.

choices.text: The emission did not change between the years $2020$ and $2024$, because the electricity production was the same in both years, $1000\,\text{GWh}$.
choices.feedback: Reading the wrong column. The number $1000\,\text{GWh}$ belongs to the column $E$, which tells the energy produced. The emission is in the column $m$, and there the value decreased from $520\,\text{kt}$ to $420\,\text{kt}$. The same production and a smaller emission mean a smaller emission per energy produced.

level3.text:
A petrol car uses $6.0$ litres per $100\,\text{km}$. The energy content of petrol is $32\,\text{MJ/}\textsf{l}$ and the emission factor of burning is $69\,\text{g/MJ}$.

An electric car uses $18\,\text{kWh}$ of electricity per $100\,\text{km}$. (The comparison is rough: for the petrol car only burning is counted, for the electric car the life-cycle emissions of the electricity.)

At what emission factor of electricity would the emission of the electric car over $100\,\text{km}$ be equal to that of the petrol car? Give the answer in the unit $\text{g/kWh}$. What does the result tell about the benefit of the electric car if the electricity is produced with coal?

An example city needs $100\,\text{GWh}$ of electricity a year and compares two ways. A solar park produces about $0.50\,\text{GWh}$ of electricity per hectare per year. A field grown for energy gives about $0.010\,\text{GWh}$ of electricity per hectare per year in a power plant. (The figures are rounded example values; $1\,\text{ha} = 0.01\,\text{km}^2$.)

How many times as large a field area would biomass electricity need compared with the area of the solar park? What does land use tell you about the ways of producing energy that the emission factor does not?

Example situation: a city bus uses $30$ litres of diesel per $100\,\text{km}$ and has $25$ passengers. The energy content of diesel is $36\,\text{MJ/}\textsf{l}$ and the emission factor of burning is $74\,\text{g/MJ}$. A petrol car driven by one person uses $6.0$ litres per $100\,\text{km}$ ($32\,\text{MJ/}\textsf{l}$ and $69\,\text{g/MJ}$). How many times as large is the emission from burning of the car per passenger compared with that of the bus?

The table shows the carbon dioxide concentration $c$ of the atmosphere in different years (yearly averages of the NOAA Mauna Loa measuring station, rounded to whole ppm values).

a) Calculate the average rate of growth of the concentration in each twenty-year period.

b) Predict the concentration in $2040$ with a straight line that continues from the point $2020$ with the rate of growth of the last period ($2000$–$2020$). Give the prediction in the unit ppm.

c) Compare the prediction with the prediction that would be obtained with the rate of growth of the whole data ($1960$–$2020$), and justify which prediction is more credible and how far a straight line can be trusted as a model.

level3.text:
The yearly electricity production of an example city is as in the table. The emission factors are from the table of the lesson: coal $820\,\text{g/kWh}$, natural gas $490\,\text{g/kWh}$, biomass $230\,\text{g/kWh}$ and wind power $12\,\text{g/kWh}$. The city plans to replace coal electricity completely: $30\,\text{GWh}$ is produced with wind power and the remaining $10\,\text{GWh}$ with natural gas, because the wind is not always enough. The energy produced stays the same. Natural sinks (the seas and vegetation) absorb only a part of the carbon dioxide emissions.

a) Calculate the present total yearly emissions in tonnes.

b) By how many per cent do the total emissions decrease in the plan? Give the answer in per cent.

c) By how many percentage points is the reduction smaller than if the whole $40\,\text{GWh}$ were produced with wind power?

d) Justify why the carbon dioxide concentration of the atmosphere can still keep growing for several years after the emissions have decreased, and name one thing that the emission factor does not tell about increasing wind electricity.
